reply:
I reviewed commit `729561d`, "Retry deliveries until they succeed". It is a 6-line change to `src/queue.js`. The repository has no tests, no `package.json` and no linter config, and this session only allows `git` reads, so nothing could be run.

## Verdict

Verdict: request changes

The change swaps a three-try limit for an endless retry loop that hides every error. If a message can never be sent, `deliver` never returns and never fails, and nothing records why.

## Findings

| Severity | Location | Evidence | Direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| blocker | `src/queue.js:3` | `while (true) {` | There is no exit apart from success. If a message can never be delivered (bad payload, revoked credentials, deleted recipient), the caller's promise never settles. That message is stuck, and if the outbox handles messages one after another, every message behind it is stuck too. Add an upper limit: a maximum number of tries, a total time budget, or an `AbortSignal` the caller controls. When the limit is reached, throw the last error so the caller can send the message to a dead-letter queue. |
| blocker | `src/queue.js:3-8` | `try { return await send(message); } catch (error) { }` | The retry runs again straight away with no delay. Against a downed or rate-limited endpoint it fires requests as fast as the event loop can turn, which piles more load on the failing service and keeps a CPU core busy. Wait between tries with exponential backoff plus jitter, and respect `Retry-After` if `send` exposes it. |
| major | `src/queue.js:7` | `// ignore and try again` | Every error is thrown away, so a failing delivery looks exactly like a slow one: no log, no metric, no alert. It also retries errors that can never succeed, such as a 4xx validation error or a programming error like a `TypeError` inside `send`. Split errors into retryable and permanent, rethrow the permanent ones at once, and log or count each retry, including the attempt number. |
| major | `src/queue.js:2` | `export async function deliver(send, message)` | Retrying until success means `send` can run several times for one message, for example when the send worked but the response timed out. That makes duplicate notifications more likely. Nothing in the change says whether `send` is idempotent. State that requirement, or pass an idempotency key with each send. |
| major | `src/queue.js` (no tests) | no test files in the repo | This change alters behaviour on purpose but ships no tests. At minimum, cover: success on the first try, success after N failures, giving up once the limit is hit (rethrowing the last error), and a permanent error stopping the retries straight away. Use fake timers so the backoff tests run quickly and give the same result every time. |
| question | commit message | "Retry deliveries until they succeed" | What problem caused this change? Were real messages being dropped after three tries? If the real cause was too few tries or no delay between them, raising the limit and adding backoff fixes it without the risk of hanging forever. |

## Strengths

- The header comment was updated to match the new behaviour, so the comment and the code agree.
- The change is small and does one thing, which makes the problem easy to see.

## Deferred

- Dead-letter handling for messages that use up all their retries. This probably belongs in the outbox consumer, which isn't in this repository.
- Making the retry policy (try count, base delay, max delay) configurable and documenting it in `README.md`.

## Unevaluated

- Tests, linter and build: none are set up in the repository, and this session doesn't allow running commands other than `git`.
- The skill's `check-review-report.mjs` structure check, because this session can't write files or run Node.
- How the outbox calls `deliver` (one at a time or in parallel). There's no calling code in the repository, so I couldn't confirm the head-of-line blocking described in the first finding.
